events.excerpt: Advocates for cloud-native software have long argued that their approach to development makes applications portable across different Kubernetes environments. But VMware argues that’s not happening across hybrid clouds, and has taken the lead in an effort to improve matters. That effort, the new Workload Conformance Working Group in the Kubernetes community, aims to establish a shared standard for how workloads run on Kubernetes. The group’s web page points out, “Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. Every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support,” the group asserts. The proposed solution? “A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.” Prashanth Shenoy, VP of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, told The Register that standard is needed in part because applications packaged to run in public clouds don’t always run well in hybrid clouds. That’s challenging for VMware, and other vendors of hybrid clouds like Nutanix and Red Hat, because they all sell tools to create and run a stack that users can deploy to both on-prem infrastructure and public clouds. VMware therefore thinks it will find support for an effort to ensure that cloud-native apps
events.title: VMware floats new standard to make sure apps don’t break in hybrid K8s environments

events.excerpt: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register : “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194 , and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review . “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants
events.title: November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs but only one zero-day so far

events.excerpt: GitHub grant application: ShieldedScan grant application · Website: https://shieldedscan.xyz · Repository: ShieldedScan · Open data: Hugging Face dataset Gm everyone! For those who don’t know it yet, Shieldedscan is a fully open-source Zcash block explorer and analytics platform, with no trackers, that I started in July this year. In just two quarters of solo development, Shieldedscan has become a complete platform, tracking the transparent pool, the shielded pools, network activity, miners, cross-chain flows, the ecosystem, ZIPs and much more. The explorer has in total 49 pages, all with a cypherpunk-style UI. I also worked early on connecting AI to Zcash data while respecting privacy. At the end of August I launched what I believe was the first Zcash AI agent, Zeno: it runs on a TEE model from NEAR AI connected to Shieldedscan’s data, so anyone can query the network in plain language while their prompts stay private. Since then, Zeno can also draw charts and tables, and export data as CSV or JSON. In October I released what, as far as I know, is the first Zcash MCP server, so anyone can use Shieldedscan’s data from any AI assistant. Shieldedscan is completely free and open: the front-end and the whole backend are open source, the data is published daily as an open dataset, and the API and MCP server are free and keyless. events.excerpt: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe , Apple , Google and Mozilla . Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969. November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device. This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes. According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194 , a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office . Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monda
events.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

events.excerpt: Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult. Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code. "Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model." Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software. Last month, Artcraft , a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5. Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA). Zhang has faced some criticism on social media for creating a limited barrier to copying other people's work (which at this point might simply be the work of another LLM). But not eve
events.title: To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them

events.excerpt: This proposal specifies the JSON document that tokenURI returns in ERC-721 and ERC-6909 and that uri returns in ERC-1155 . Most deployed tokens already use this format, but only part of it was ever specified. ERC-721 and ERC-1155 define name , description and image . Everything else wallets and marketplaces show ( animation_url , attributes and its display_type values, external_url , background_color ) comes from a page OpenSea published in 2018. Clients fill the gaps differently, so the same token renders differently from one app to the next. Draft: erc-8495.md ( ethereum/ERCs#2163 ) The draft covers: Every field and its type, every display_type value in use, and what clients do with values that don’t match, such as booleans, quoted numbers and dates in milliseconds. The URI schemes clients must resolve ( https , ipfs , ar , data ), the ones they may resolve ( ipns , and web3 from ERC-4804 ), and the ones they must never resolve. Fetching rules: ipfs:// URIs instead of gateway URLs, sandboxing HTML in animation_url , and keeping server-side fetches away from private addresses. How later proposals add fields without breaking older clients. The Rationale cites an October 2026 survey of 708 Ethereum and Base contracts. 113 of the 204 IPFS gateway URLs in it failed when fetched as written, and more contracts use text as a display_type than string . The draft accepts both. Questions we’d like input on: Data URIs. The draft recommends base64, because fetch drops everything after # in an unencoded data URL, which breaks JSON that contains a # . Clients must accept base64 and shou
events.title: ERC-8495: Token Metadata JSON Schema

events.excerpt: The Mozilla-backed Thunderbird project is getting closer to a wider launch of a hosted email service designed to complement its desktop mail app. Now known as Thundermail (what else?), the service was originally developed under the Thunderbird Pro banner, which encompassed paid email, appointment scheduling, and file-sharing services designed to generate additional revenue for the organization. The org has been inviting people from its Thundermail waitlist to try the service through an early-access program, and this writer just happened to be among them. Thundermail offers a web-based email interface and can also be accessed through the Thunderbird desktop app, the Thunderbird mobile app for Android, or other compatible email clients. The Thunderbird apps remain free. Users get an inbox with up to 15 email addresses and three custom domains, plus 30 GB of mail storage and 60 GB of send storage for Thunderbird Send, an end-to-end encrypted file-sharing and large-attachment service. That’s for starters – the org intends to offer those extra features and services at different price points. Yes, Thundermail is a paid service, which may put off some users who are used to free email accounts offered via Gmail, Outlook.com and Proton Mail, but with the first two of those you do get served ads along with your messages. The sign-up screens for Thundermail suggest the basic service will cost $6 per month, billed annually. This is roughly equivalent to the £55 we paid for a year on the early access program. We asked Thunderbird when we can expect to see Thundermail officially launched
events.title: Mozilla Thunderbird email service edges closer to launch with early access

events.excerpt: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally. A malicious server can supply a name cont
events.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced

events.excerpt: After teasing its 256-core Epycs for more than a year, AMD is finally ready to talk about architectural changes to the Zen core that not only make it possible, but will eventually power its next generation of Ryzen processors in desktop and mobile PCs. During a press event in Las Vegas last week, AMD spilled the beans on its latest Zen cores, which promise an average 27 percent uplift in instructions per clock (IPC) across a variety of AI and server workloads, along with boosted clocks ranging from 4.1 to 5.3 GHz. We expect to see even higher frequencies on consumer chips before long, but AMD isn’t quite ready to talk about Ryzen just yet. CPU performance is a function of power, IPC, and clocks, and with gains across all three, the cores are shaping up to be one of the company’s biggest generational jumps ever. A tale of two cores As in past Epyc launches, Zen 6 isn’t one core. It comes in two flavors: a frequency-optimized variant (Zen 6) and a density-optimized version (Zen 6c). This split dates back to the launch of AMD’s Bergamo Epycs in 2023, which packed 128 compact Zen 4c cores into just eight chiplets. The chip’s debut drew comparisons to Intel’s still relatively new Efficient (E-cores) for obvious reasons. But under the hood, AMD’s Zen 4c was nothing like what Intel was doing. The core itself was nearly identical to Zen 4; it simply traded clocks and a bit of cache per core for a more densely packed CPU die. The only difference between running an application on Bergamo or Genoa was how quickly it executed. The same could not be said of Intel’s P and E cores, which
events.title: AMD winds up Zen 6 cores for faster clock speeds

events.excerpt: AMD's upcoming Verano processors aren't like any Epyc CPUs we've seen before. Rather than general-purpose workloads, Verano is designed specifically to power AMD's next generation of GPU servers. In an interview with The Register during a press event in Las Vegas last week, Madhu Rangarajan, corporate VP of AMD's compute and enterprise AI products business, described Verano as being the first step towards building something that more closely resembles Nvidia's Vera Rubin superchips. "Verano is really designed for an integrated CPU+GPU rack scale solution," he said. "From that perspective, I wouldn't say the CPU is a competitor to Vera. In a head note, I'd say the Verano+GPU solution is a competitor to Vera+Rubin." For reference, Vera Rubin and the GB200 and GB300 that came before it aren't your typical server platforms. Instead they're more like an enormous single-board computer combining CPUs and GPUs into a tightly-integrated package. Each of Nvidia's superchips joins a single 88-core Vera CPU and 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X memory to a pair of Rubin GPUs via Nvidia's speedy NVLink-C2C interconnect. Rangarajan tells us Verano will be the host CPU for a similar class of product using AMD GPUs, and much like Nvidia's superchips, the CPU will also use notebook memory rather than conventional RDIMMS. However, unlike Vera, which is also being deployed as a standalone CPU in storage servers and agent sandboxes, Verano has a singular purpose: keeping its GPUs fed. (We assume they'll be MI500X GPUs.) This design choice reflects AMD's philosophy of one SKU per workload. As such, Verano's co
events.title: A closer look at Verano, AMD's first step toward a Zen-based superchip to rival Nvidia's Vera Rubin

events.excerpt: The UK Post Office is extending its contract with Fujitsu to give it time to move services to a new supplier, after a scandal that has long marred the relationship between the two. The current contract runs until March 2027, and the publicly owned company has announced a short, time-limited contract extension to cover the transition. Accenture will take over running the Horizon system, which was at the center of a string of miscarriages of justice, from September 2027, after winning a £410 million contract in May this year. Meanwhile, the Post Office is developing a replacement for the aging system to serve its network of 11,500 branches. The Post Office began rolling out the legacy Horizon IT system for accounting in 1999, along with two subsequent upgrades. The electronic point-of-sale (EPOS) and back-end finance system was first implemented by ICL, a UK tech firm majority-owned by Fujitsu in the 1990s and which it fully acquired in 1998 . From 1999 until 2015, around 736 subpostmasters were wrongfully prosecuted and convicted over Horizon errors, devastating lives in the process. The Post Office, Accenture, and Fujitsu have agreed that Fujitsu will hand over the operation of Horizon to Accenture between 1 June and 1 September 2027, with the final date set to be confirmed in March 2027. Accenture is set to "walk in and take over" the current Horizon system by assuming day-to-day operations from Fujitsu, as well as developing the back-end of the new system to replace Horizon. Post Office CEO Neil Brocklehurst said: "Ending our contract with Fujitsu is a critical milestone
events.title: Another contract extension for Fujitsu on the Post Office's Horizon

events.excerpt: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine. events.excerpt: Between 12 and 13 million UK smart meters could stop working properly when 2G and 3G networks are switched off by 2033, and replacing them all is likely to cost around £4 billion ($5.3 billion). Smart meters have long been a controversial topic thanks to the British government's botched rollout of the technology; they were supposed to be fitted into 80 percent of households by 2020. But numerous delays and technical hitches, such as consumers finding their meter stopped being smart if they switched energy supplier , hindered progress. Now, a report from connectivity biz Wirepas, "The European Connectivity Trilemma," shows that it isn't just Brits who have problems, but that other European countries also have their share of smart meter issues and that no two countries have adopted the same approach. The UK's issues center on the fact that early meters used 2G or 3G cellular connections to transmit energy usage back to the supplier. These continued to be fitted until 4G versions began arriving at the end of 2024, the report says. This issue was covered by The Register back in 2023 , and again in 2024 . However, the government had already announced measures to phase out 2G and 3G networks by 2033 several years earlier, back in 2021, so it was known that any meters being fitted would have a limited lifespan. In fact, 3G services have now already been withdrawn by the networks , and they all plan to phase out 2G ahead of the 2033 deadline . events.excerpt: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet , thereby validating the design of libsignal 's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review. The result is theoretical in that
events.title: Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques

events.excerpt: Microsoft will enable access to Anthropic's Claude models by default for UK Copilot tenants next month, giving administrators a deadline to decide whether US-based processing fits their compliance requirements. From December 9, UK tenants whose administrators have not already chosen a setting will have Claude access enabled. Administrators can disable it, but leaving the setting untouched means opting in. In this instance, Anthropic operates as a Microsoft subprocessor , and Claude models are already on by default for most customers in the Windows giant's commercial cloud. The exceptions, notably, include the European Union, the European Free Trade Association, and the UK. However, UK tenants aren't in scope for Microsoft's EU Data Boundary - launched at the start of 2023 - and so Redmond is flipping the switch for the country. Anthropic processes the relevant data in the United States, Microsoft's documentation states . Administrators therefore have until December 9 to review whether that meets their organization's data-handling requirements and set access accordingly. Microsoft is also retiring the setting that restricts Claude access to Microsoft 365 alone. "This affirms Microsoft's commitment to offering choice between leading AI models while maintaining enterprise-grade security and compliance," the Redmond-based biz said. So long as you don't mind processing happening in the US. ®

events.excerpt: The European Union has dragged IBM, Atos, and Leonardo into court over years of delays to its troubled €212 million smart border system, which finally went live after missing a string of deadlines and leaving travelers stuck in airport queues. The lawsuit dates back to December 22, 2025, when eu-LISA, the agency behind the EU's fingerprint-and-facial-image border checks for non-EU travelers, filed its claim in an Estonian court. The Financial Times has since named the three companies after obtaining letters exchanged with the agency. "The proceedings concern the system’s development phase and have no impact on its current operation. events.excerpt: Security researchers exploited flaws in Android apps to gain remote access to connected cars from two major automakers, allowing them to start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns. Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year. By tinkering with the cars’ Android apps, they devised exploit paths to issue remote commands to vehicles in Australia and the US . The pair published separate blogs covering different aspects of the research; Shah said the US attack "required a lot more work" because the automaker "spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments." Both exploit chains centered around weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity platform relied upon by both automakers, the identities of which were kept anonymous by the researchers, who have previously highlighted flaws in the likes of Hyundai , Kia , Subaru , and many others . In the Australian version of the app, the researchers first found a vehicle identification number (VIN) using public licence plate checkers, and used those in queries to internal APIs, which provided personal information and owner email addresses. They also found hardcoded admin credentials for the ForgeRock OpenIDM that were meant for the staging environment but also worked in production. After bypassing the heavy WAF filtering by exploiting path traversal flaws, they were able to invoke the internal admin APIs and take over target accounts using only their email addresses. This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send
events.title: Researchers pwn automakers’ Android apps to remotely unlock cars, honk horns

events.excerpt: Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave. World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes. Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus." The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom " nature makes no leaps ," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference. Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time." Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture ( JEPA ) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action. But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to antic
events.title: Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions

events.excerpt: NASA is moving ahead with its plan to repurpose a Mars rover engineering model as a lunar trundlebot for less than $400 million. The robot, dubbed PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), is a cut-and-shut of engineering test articles used for the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers, currently rolling around the Red Planet. During a weekend briefing , NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith. Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components. Blue Origin is to deposit the rover on the Moon. NASA awarded the company a $94 million base contract, "with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole." The figures make it difficult to ascertain the exact cost of the PROMISE mission. However, during the briefing, NASA said it had "a pretty firm agreement with JPL to basically deliver the rover to the surface under $400 million." The $400 million includes the lander, which will be Blue Origin's Mark 1. Earlier this year, The Planetary S

events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. The end of the bytecode is the other place it breaks. solc appends the IPFS hash of the metadata file, and the metadata holds a hash of every source file, so a changed comment changes the tail. I tried it on a small contract with one immutable: adding one comment line changed exactly the 32 bytes of that hash and nothing else. If everything matches except the tail, the compiled logic is the same but the sources are not the ones
events.title: Checking that a deployed contract still runs the audited commit

events.excerpt: I read the upgrade control of 7 tokenized treasury and gold fund tokens on Ethereum straight from the chain. Snapshot: 9 Nov 2026. Read-only; nothing was tested on live contracts. Result (7 tokens I looked at, not a market ranking): 3: the upgrade owner is one externally owned address (no contract code), no on-chain delay 2: Safe multisig, 4-of-7, no delay found 1: older multisig, 3-of-6, no delay found 1: timelock, 24h minimum delay What this does NOT say: that any key is stored badly (it may sit behind HSM/MPC or issuer processes that are invisible from outside), that assets are at risk, or that other controls (pauses, legal, off-chain) are missing. It only shows who can change token code on-chain. How to reproduce with any public RPC. Three patterns cover all 7: A) EIP-1967 proxy: read the admin slot, then ask the admin for its owner. cast storage <token> 0xb53127684a568b3173ae13b9f8a6016e243e63b6e8ee1178d6a717850b5d6103 cast call <admin> "owner()(address)" B) Owner stored on the token/proxy itself: cast call <token> "owner()(address)" C) Older proxy admin slot: cast storage <token> 0x10d6a54a4754c8869d6886b5f5d7fbfa5b4522237ea5c60d11bc4e7a1ff9390b Then check what the owner is: cast code <owner> # empty = externally owned getThreshold() # Safe getMinDelay() # timelock I am not naming the tokens: this is about the pattern, not about any one issuer. Questions I would like feedback on: is “no on-chain delay” the right thing to flag for tokenized funds, and what other control signals (pause roles, mint/burn roles) would be worth adding to a standard check? Short version on X
events.title: Who can upgrade 7 tokenized treasury/gold tokens on Ethereum? A read-only look at upgrade control

events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX). The test takes 30 seconds and uses no API keys. The full methodology, results, and test script are at The Short Version — The Rogue Wave — sections 17 and 18. What needs to change: The per-asset threshold model must be replaced with a joint probability model that accounts for tail correlation acro
events.title: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

Reference repository: GitHub - garyyang-finchip/agent-meditation-mechanism: Agent Meditation Mechanism · GitHub . Sepolia evidence: recorded in the repository and summarized in a reply below. This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. events.excerpt: Summary. AIFP is a framework ERC for the information layer between agents. It defines a flow paradigm as a content-addressed, versioned description of an interaction context - which carriers (addressed delivery, shared object) and structural operators (fan-out, fan-in, feedback, n-party, select, forward, derive, merge) it uses, and how thirteen separately declared rule dimensions are set (discovery, observation, contribution, management, redistribution, history, time, disclosure timing, contributor visibility, admission basis, representation, object relations, ordering). A channel adopts exactly one paradigm version at any timepoint. Participation is recorded as separately addressable role bindings with a scope, a basis, a validity interval and the rule version they were granted under. Role acquisition is checked by composable predicates that answer one of four outcomes: satisfied, not satisfied, undeterminable, verifier error. Status. Draft. events.excerpt: Summary As part of regular governance upkeep, Uniswap Labs reviews the protocol infrastructure that governance owns and brings forward improvements as they are needed. This RFC proposes two technical updates: Upgrade the VolatilePair Hook on Ethereum Update the protocol fee releaser on X Layer Below we outline the background and proposed changes for both initiatives. Part 1: VolatilePair Hook Upgrade Background VolatilePair Hook is a Uniswap v4 dynamic-fee hook built by Uniswap Labs. It went live on Ethereum on October 14 with the ETH/USDC pool and has since launched on Robinhood Chain (ETH/USDG). Volatile pairs did more than $500 billion in volume on Uniswap this year. In a static-fee pool, when the price moves elsewhere, LPs end up absorbing the cost while the pool quotes a stale price and someone else trades against it to keep the difference. VolatilePair Hook prices both sides of the trade, setting separate buy and sell fees on every swap: When the pool price rises, buying costs more and selling costs less. When pool price falls, the fees flip. After a large price move, trades that push the price back pay a temporary fee . VolatilePair Hook was designed to keep value in the pool while quoting a competitive spread, enabling stronger and more consistent returns for LPs. The hook is an upgradeable proxy contract owned by Uniswap Governance, so the mechanism can be improved without pools needing to migrate. This proposal is the first use of that upgrade path. events.excerpt: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity This is an announcement of the research article with the same title and a brief informal intro for ethresear.ch. A classic approach to tackling MEV in decentralized exchanges on Ethereum is to enable a mechanism that receives trade orders during a block interval and settles all the swaps in a batch following a fairness criterion. It is an old problem. I imagine that an informed reader might feel somewhat skeptical. Thoughts of this kind were expressed in 2014 in this Reddit post . CoW Swap, UniswapX, 1inch’s Fusion, Sorella’s Angstrom, and Propellerheads’ Turbine have all tackled the problem using batch trading in one way or another. Walraswap started in 2023 at Flashbots, independently of the previous and closely related work by Ramseyer, Goyal, Goel, and Mazières: Augmenting Batch Exchanges… and SPEEDEX . The central feature in common: we treat the DEX problem from the point of view of the theory of equilibrium for an exchange economy with n tokens. To understand equilibrium in two sentences: given a finite set of trade orders, under mild hypotheses and neglecting transaction costs, there exists a price vector —an equilibrium — at which all the orders can be executed with no deficit or surplus of any token. Some of the orders may trade nothing at equilibrium. What’s special about Walraswap? First note that none of the Ethereum DEXs mentioned above are based on equilibrium. Not even CoW Swap, which for many years adopted the similar but weaker property of uniform clearing prices . We can

events.excerpt: v2.11.0 is a hardfork, security and stability release on top of v2.10.3 . It's the public release of v2.11.0-priv , which validators and major RPC providers already run. Uburu hardfork Already active on both networks: Network Fork block Amoy 51978200 Mainnet 96787900 Uburu updates the StateReceiver genesis contract ( 0x…1001 ) at the fork block. It changes how state syncs are executed and recorded. Operators on v2.11.0-priv : same code, switch to v2.11.0 at your next maintenance window. Nodes still on v2.10.3 or older stopped following the chain at the fork block. Upgrade immediately. Highlights Consensus and state sync : state-sync records are fetched from Heimdall one page at a time, as the per-block budget admits them. A failed fetch now fails the block, where before it committed it without state syncs. Span lookups by block number follow Heimdall's rule (the highest-id span containing the block). Locally sealed blocks are checked against whitelisted milestones before they're written. Header verification bounds block numbers and base fees on every import path. Execution : BlockSTM bounds speculative work per block and falls back to serial execution when the bound is hit. Stateless / witnesses : witness messages are bounded on receive, and witness-caused import failures are charged to the peer that served the witness. State serving : snap range serving and state iterators no longer read superseded state layers. Txpool : PIP-15 conditional transactions are off by default. Overdraft checks count queued transactions that will be promoted. RPC and log index : eth_feeHistory n

events.excerpt: Proposal Type : Ratification Executive Summary This Ratification vote adds an Upgrade Authority Transfer policy to the Governing Policies section of the Standard Rollup Charter. It sets out how a Chain Governor may request that upgrade authority for its chain be transferred from the Security Council to an address of its choosing, so the chain can manage upgrades itself or through a third party. Under the policy, the Optimism Foundation confirms a valid request and publishes a public notice on the Governance Forum. After a mandatory 30-day notice period, the Security Council is directed to execute the transfer. Once the transfer is executed, the chain ceases to be a Standard Rollup. This is a non-fork upgrade. It changes Charter language only: no smart contract or node software changes are required, and this proposal executes no onchain transactions. Motivation The Standard Rollup Charter defines how a chain becomes a Standard Rollup, including authorizing the Security Council to perform upgrades. It does not define how a chain leaves. Today, a Chain Governor that wants to take back upgrade authority has no published path, and any transfer would require ad hoc governance action. This gap matters for three reasons: Predictability for Chain Governors. Handing upgrade authority to the Security Council is a significant commitment. Chain Governors, particularly enterprises with formal risk and procurement reviews, need to know before they commit how they could exit. events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10595v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The limited computational resources of Internet of Things (IoT) devices present challenges for secure image processing. This paper presents a distributed chaotic image encryption system using independent Wi-Fi-connected ESP32-S3 microcontrollers. A master-worker architecture distributes image blocks through master-coordinated chaotic sequence management, maintaining one logically continuous chaotic sequence by assigning block-specific starting states independently of worker assignments. The implemented system uses reversible chaotic substitution (SUBSTITUTE), while Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)-signed discovery messages and Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 with mutual authentication secure device communication. Experimental evaluation using one, two, and four workers demonstrates a reduction in execution time from 43.215 to 15.878 seconds, achieving a speed-up of 2.72 times. The encrypted image achieves a Shannon entropy of 7.999940 bits/byte and near-zero adjacent-pixel correlation. Exact image recovery is verified through matching Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) hashes and a Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) value of 1.0. Additional experiments demonstrate successful encryption and decryption using different worker counts and block sizes, automatic task reassignment following worker failure, and rejection of a mismatched private key during TLS authentication. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of secure, flexible, and distributed chaotic image processing across independent resource
events.title: Design and Evaluation of Secure Distributed Chaotic Image Encryption on ESP32-S3

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11399v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) present significant challenges to source tracing of generated code, as LLM rewriting can substantially alter the syntactic and structural characteristics of watermarked code. However, existing watermarking methods often suffer severe performance degradation under LLM-based functionality-preserving rewriting attacks. We attribute this vulnerability not merely to the intensity of rewriting, but to a fundamental distribution mismatch between the perturbations encountered during watermark training and the global, non-deterministic rewriting behaviors induced by LLMs. In order to deal with this challenge, we propose RoCoMark, a Robust Code waterMarking framework that explicitly learns and adapts to LLM rewriting behaviors. RoCoMark is a multi-round minimax game between the watermark embedder and LLM rewriter. In each round, the embedder first learns threat profiling from LLM-rewritten code by optimizing the watermark encoder through contrastive learning and knowledge distillation while mitigating catastrophic representation drift. Then the embedder improves strategies by optimizing the watermark encoder and extractor simultaneously. Finally, an adaptive attack-evolution mechanism based on Reflexion and short- and long-term memory pools is applied, enabling continuous interaction between the watermark embedder and evolving rewriting strategies. This iterative attacker-defender process progressively improves the robustness of the watermark against diverse and previously unseen LLM rewriting behaviors.
events.title: RoCoMark: Robust Code Watermarking Against LLM-Based Functionality-Preserving Rewriting Attacks

events.excerpt: Server consolidation has led Cisco to boost the speed of top-of-rack switches to 100G. The networking giant last week announced the catchily named N9348C8D-H2, a 1U device packing 48 100G SFP-DD ports and eight 400G QSFP-DD uplinks. At the Cisco Live event in Melbourne, Australia, this week, Cisco’s senior veep for datacenter and internet infrastructure, Kevin Wollenweber, said one reason the company created the device is that modern servers often feature a pair of fast network interface cards. The twin cards are needed because sixth-gen server processors from Intel and AMD offer dozens, or even hundreds, of physical processor cores and therefore generate a lot of traffic. The density of computing power those processors provide has led chipmakers and server manufacturers to suggest replacing handfuls of machines running older, power-guzzling Xeons and Epycs with boxes running more efficient sixth-gen chips. The Register hears it’s not uncommon to achieve 6:1 server consolidation ratios when moving from third- or fourth-generation Xeons or Epycs to current models. Users who make that move can pack many more server cores into the same rack. Power bills go down, but the quantity of data leaving a rack goes up. Wollenweber said Cisco realized it had “tons” of switches that offer 25G ports but felt it had a gap in its range for non-AI scenarios like server consolidation that produced increased data flows. The exec admitted that the 100G ports may be overkill for a modest collection of new servers, but argued users recognize it won’t be long before they grow into the excess capac
events.title: Ye olde server consolidation has made Cisco push top-of-rack switching to 100G

events.excerpt: Hi all — EnsRationis from Robonomics. Sensors.social is an open environmental data network I designed, and it is now growing across the EU. Everything is open source: the Altruist sensors that feed it, the software that collects the readings, and the map. Web3 does one job here, the one it is good at: it settles the data as a common good anyone can check, not a vendor’s database. How it works on Robonomics Owners who choose to share their Altruist’s data join the network; each sensor has its own key and signs every measurement it sends. A connectivity node checks the signature and that the sensor has an active subscription on Robonomics, a parachain on Polkadot, then passes the reading to the live map. The node collects readings into batches, stores each batch on IPFS and writes its hash to Robonomics. Anyone can fetch a batch and check it against the chain. The network is federated: a city or a lab can run its own connectivity node, and its sensors still show up on the common map. Next, with Robonomics 5.0: the reading the sensor signed goes on chain itself, so there is no need to trust the node at all. Try the map: https://sensors.social Happy to hear from anyone who wants to run a sensor in their city or build on the data. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
events.title: Sensors.social: an open air-quality network on Polkadot is growing across the EU

events.excerpt: Built by a 14-year-old developer, a new tool called Autark treats AI agents as a virtual team that can work without constant prompting. Users put tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent delegates them to other agents that carry out the work and report their results. Agents can also ask clarifying questions if tasks are too vague. “Agents do not wait for a prompt,” Autark’s website explains . “A schedule, a timer, a new task, a message or an event wakes them up. They decide what to do, do it, and can plan their own next step.” As one would hope from a product like this, Autark is model agnostic and can be set up to connect to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services’ CLI tools. Local models are also supported. Your mileage may vary if you choose to use anything besides Codex or Claude Code, though, as Autark’s website mentions support for other models is built in but hasn’t been tested in a live run yet, as Autark is still under active development as an open-source tool. Real teenage engineering Autark is the brainchild of teenage Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees. He’s still in school, and tells The Register he’s deeply interested in AI and came up with Autark after being unhappy with existing AI tools. “I could get help with individual tasks, but I still had to organise the work, remember what was unfinished and keep pushing it forward,” Hees said of his time using Claude Code and Codex. “I wanted a system that could take responsibility for ongoing work, not just respond to my next message.” He developed Autark - or,

events.excerpt: AMD's cache-packed Epyc X chips are officially making a comeback. Based on the House of Zen's frequency-optimized SKUs we looked at back in September , its HPC-optimized Venice-X parts will offer up to 96 cores and use the company's 3D V-Cache chip stack tech to triple the L3 cache density to more than a gigabyte. But before you get too excited about another cache-packed Epyc, it'll be a little while before they actually ship. AMD expects the Venice-X to begin trickling out in the second half of 2027. First teased at CES earlier this year, the chips are primarily aimed at latency-sensitive technical and scientific computing workloads like computational fluid dynamics and electronic design automation (EDA). AMD itself relies heavily on its X-series Epycs for EDA workloads like functional verification testing, which is used to simulate silicon in order to ensure it behaves as it's intended to. According to AMD Fellow Phil Steinke, by keeping more of the model in cache, the CPU cores don't have to wait as long for data to move in and out of system memory. Normally, boosting L3 capacity would have required larger chiplets with lower yields, but that's not how AMD has gone about it for the past four years. Instead, it used advanced packaging to give its existing CPU dies a little SRAM backpack. This tech has been around for several generations now, having first debuted in the Ryzen 7 5800X3D back in 2022. That consumer desktop chip stacked a 64 MB SRAM tile on top of an 8-core chiplet, boosting L3 capacity to 96 MB. The extra cache made the chip one of the most potent gaming CPU
events.title: AMD's Epyc X-chips are back after a three-year hiatus

events.excerpt: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination , announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024 , having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit. CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports . It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February. With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. The 2026 AI100 Study Panel report acknowledges its limitations in its twelfth takeaway: "This report will be out of date by the time you read it." But it's nonetheless a worthwhile exercise for those who haven't been paying close attention to the development of machine learning over the past few years and for policymakers who may benefit from a review of AI's metastatic growth. " This report examines what led to the extraordinary capabilities of today's AI systems, and how they are reshaping society. As we look ahead, we anticipate continued increase in AI capabilities alongside transformative advances in science and medicine. "Rapid change will challenge governments and industry to support and safeguard our people, our institutions, and our critical infrastructure. Both the benefits and the risks of AI technologies require the same clear-eyed scrutiny." Established in 2014, the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is overseen by a Standing Committee of AI experts and administered by Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). events.excerpt: We propose an institution-managed user payment ledger for recording account debits and credits, enforcing spending capacity, and sealing account periods independently of funds settlement. Specification Draft PR #2159 Problem and scope A payment institution needs to distinguish a customer’s business entries from changes to the spending capacity it grants. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. This proposal defines a common contract interface for those records and controls. It can serve an institution’s own business independently or compose with an on-chain payment protocol. It does not issue or transfer assets, establish customer identity, or prove that funds have been frozen or settled. Account model and interface Each account is scoped by (account, institution) . An institution can serve payer accounts, merchant accounts, or both; the same address at two institutions does not share records or capacity. Holding the account’s private key does not grant permission to write entries. Current state contains a limit baseline, cumulative outflows and inflows, and a user-period identifier: available = limit + credit - debit The three amounts and the resulting available capacity must fit in uint96 ; arithmetic uses wider intermediates and rejects negative capacity or out-of-range results. Five write operations separate the relevant responsibilities: addLimit and subLimit adjust the baseline without changing business-entry totals
events.title: ERC-8494: Institution-Managed User Payment Ledger

events.excerpt: The prdoc for the XCMv3 removal ( pr_13629.prdoc ) has a line the announcement here doesn’t have: “Assets trapped under a v3 hash become unclaimable.” I wanted to know how much that is on Polkadot, so I pulled every AssetsTrapped event for the relay and Asset Hub from Statescan and checked each hash against AssetTraps storage today. On the relay, 299 trap entries from the v3 period are still unclaimed, with 673.7 DOT in them. On Asset Hub there are 177, with 263.2 DOT and a bit of USDT and USDC. On both chains the v3 period runs from June 2023 to April 2024, when the runtimes moved to v4. Most of it belongs to ordinary accounts, not parachains. That’s 636.9 DOT across 224 accounts on the relay and 262.6 DOT across 116 accounts on Asset Hub. How it got there All but one of those account traps came from limitedTeleportAssets between the relay and Asset Hub. On the relay, most of the ones I opened show KilledAccount , then AssetsTrapped , then Attempted failing with FailedToTransactAsset . The account sent its whole balance, got reaped in the same transaction, and what the program had withdrawn went into the trap. On Asset Hub they fail with the same error, but the accounts weren’t reaped and most still hold DOT. A wallet team asked about these here in May 2024, and the answer then was claim_assets with the exact assets from the event. Why the removal ends it pallet-xcm stores a trap as a count under blake2_256(origin, VersionedAssets) , so the version is part of the key. claim_assets reads the version from the assets you pass and makes it the ticket, GeneralIndex(3) for these

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, AI agents now take on paid work on-chain. The client locks the pay in an escrow, and the escrow pays the agent when the work is accepted. As this grows, each payment also has to cover others: a tax that funds public services, a fee to whoever referred the job, or the repayment of a loan the agent took to do the job. This is a draft ERC for Settlement Deductions . It lets an escrow withhold these amounts from each payout. The escrow does not need to know the rules behind them. None of them can stall the payout. It works for any task escrow, not only those used by agents. Example: a payout of 100, with a 1% tax, a 2% referral fee and a repayment of 30. The treasury gets 1, the referrer 2, the lender 30. The payee gets 67. Repository (draft text, reference policy, example escrow, tests): GitHub - unicore-gpu/settlement-deductions: Draft ERC: settlement deductions for task escrows (tax, referral fees, repayments withheld at payout, never stalling settlement) · GitHub The ERC text is ERC-draft.md in the repository. I will open the PR to ethereum/ERCs next, with this thread as its discussion link. The slot this fills Escrows for agent work end in one transfer to the payee. The token-bound task tender draft (ERC-8414) pays the fulfiller on acceptance, verification or timeout. ERC-8183 releases the budget to the provider when the evaluator completes the job. events.excerpt: Hi everyone, We built a prototype to see what it would take for a Zcash node to verify a STARK proof for an L2 batch. We wanted to measure the cost to the node and identify what a future transaction format would need to specify. STARK verification through Transparent Zcash Extensions (TZEs) was considered for NU7. The Zcash Foundation’s polling recap found insufficient support for including it and called for further discussion of the use case and design. NU7 shipped without a new transaction format. We ran our experiment on a separate local Regtest network with Zebra v7, NU7 rules, and an experimental transaction extension. NU7 polling recap · NU7 deployment specification What ran on Regtest We built a Rust verifier and integrated it into Zebra. A small Cairo token ledger uses the extension to submit batches. Each accepted batch spends the output that records the previous ledger state and creates a new one. Both nodes check the Stwo proof before accepting the transition. In two full test runs, both nodes accepted six chained batches per run. We tested deposit claims, L2 transfers, withdrawals, re-proving a batch after a reorg, and continuing after a node restarted from finalized state. The 4:45 demo follows four batches. With the sequencer stopped, we rebuild the ledger from on-chain data, generate a withdrawal proof, and mine the transaction. Zebra also rejects two variants before accepting the valid transaction. One has a single bit flipped in the proof. The other pays one zatoshi below the prototype’s fee threshold. Watch the Regtest demo What we measured Metric Result P

events.excerpt: Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship. Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments. “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions. Qubole did not respond to The Register 's inquiries. Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles. events.excerpt: Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings. It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter. Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior. However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again. Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up. You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently. It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to re
events.title: Microsoft takes three decades to make Sticky Keys less sticky

events.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for EIP-8487 (PR: Add EIP: Separate execution credits and billing credits by Giulio2002 · Pull Request #12637 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub ). The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. Open questions: the exact schedules, charge points, rebate rules, receipt fields and block accounting. Feedback welcome. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic
events.title: EIP-8487: Separate execution credits and billing credits

events.excerpt: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking. Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on. Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release. The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1. There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident , tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another. events.title: Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session

events.excerpt: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia. In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register , the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider. The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on. The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper. Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question. "We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse. In a separate public statement , Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffith
events.title: Who Gives A Crap? Hackers, apparently, after toilet paper maker's customer data exposed

events.excerpt: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices. Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash. "Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins. "About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs." Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare. Its latest report, " An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent ," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register , have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use. At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources
events.title: The AI bubble can wait, but your exit plan can't

events.excerpt: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required . Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's requirments, email began flowing once more. SPF m
events.title: Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways

events.excerpt: In October 2025, Vitalik’s GKR tutorial was my first encounter with GKR. Its central observation, that the protocol commits only to a circuit’s input and output and never to the layers in between, made GKR look like the natural tool for proving hash-heavy computation. A year later, that has led to what is, as far as we know, the first machine-checked soundness bound for GKR on general layered circuits, in Isabelle/HOL. The same work produced a soundness proof for sparse-Merkle updates built on that bound, a partial refinement that ties the model to the Rust code, and a sparse prover whose release 1.2 proves 2.41–2.71× faster with byte-identical proofs and unchanged Isabelle theories. This post follows that work, StateSync-GKR, from the protocol and its field to the update a circuit encodes, the Rust code and the prover arithmetic. Two arXiv papers give the details: Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates, with a Machine-Checked Core and StateSync-GKR: Design and Evaluation of a Reusable Sparse GKR Engine , whose appendix plots the measurements in 363 panels. All formal results are proved in the first paper, and Isabelle/HOL also checks the parts marked as machine-checked. The main results: The first machine-checked GKR soundness bound for general layered circuits, with a cube gate. For circuits with linear, product and cube gates, Isabelle/HOL checks the bound (s_out + Σᵢ(2sᵢ·db(sᵢ) + 1))/|𝔽| for the whole layer chain and any layer polynomial of total degree at most db(sᵢ), on top of the sumcheck formalization in the Archive of Formal Proofs (dates in Sectio

events.excerpt: TL;DR: An opt-in, public, per-account “protected” flag for ERC-20s. Small sends stay instant; anything bigger is scheduled and can be cancelled by a pre-registered backup wallet; a “stress” action sweeps everything to the backup and locks it, which also helps against wrench attacks. Turning protection on is instant; weakening it (off, higher limit, shorter waits, new backup) takes a delay the holder picks. Why: Today a stolen key or a coerced holder means an instant, final drain. Existing approaches are per-transfer (SLOW), need recipient cooperation (ERC-8236), need judges (ERC-20R), protect protocols rather than users (ERC-7265), or only work in one smart wallet. This puts the protection in the token, so it works for any holder and any wallet, including plain EOAs. How it works: protect(backup, dailyLimit, holdWindow, offDelay, lockDuration, fastLane) : instant. Over-limit transferFrom reverts (never returns true without moving tokens, so routers, vaults and lenders can’t be fooled). Over-limit transfer from an EOA may be auto-scheduled, so wallet “Send” buttons just work. queueTransfer → hold window → anyone can executeTransfer ; the owner or backup can cancelTransfer ; with the opt-in fast lane, the backup can approveTransfer to skip the wait. stress(account) : cancels everything pending and moves the balance to the backup, locked for a preconfigured duration (the caller can’t choose it, so a coerced caller can’t pick zero). Receiving is always instant; unprotected accounts are plain ERC-20. Status: We built a working reference implementation at ETHGlobal Mumbai: a 1:1

events.excerpt: Description Clean builds of sui-node are slow: about 164s in dev and about 296s in release on a 16-core Mac. This cuts them to about 130s in dev and about 231s in release without removing functionality. Each commit stands alone: Drop unneeded crates from the graph. sui-simulator re-exported Move package and build crates that nothing used. These pulled move-compiler and sui-sdk into the build. sui-indexer-alt-metrics now puts its postgres collector behind a postgres feature, so diesel and postgres are no longer built. No host build of sui-types for a build script. sui-package-management 's build.rs now reads the snapshot manifest JSON directly instead of depending on sui-framework-snapshot . Less code generation in sui-core . Spawn helpers box futures before tokio::spawn , so tokio compiles one task harness instead of one per future type. This costs one extra allocation per spawn. typed-store 's DBMap / SafeIter methods move the code that doesn't depend on the key and value types into non-generic functions. SuiNode::start_async returns a boxed future, so node startup compiles once in the sui-node library instead of again in the binary. rocksdb no longer waits for jemalloc. rocksdb's jemalloc feature only enables jemalloc's unprefixed malloc. The C++ define it adds isn't read by rocksdb's sources. typed-store now turns on that jemalloc feature directly, so rocksdb's C++ build script starts without waiting for jemalloc's. The resolved jemalloc features are the same as before. Test plan Covered by existing tests for the changed crates. Timings come from alternating clean cargo

events.excerpt: How large can EIP-8141’s validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark Authors: Stefano De Angelis , Daniil Ankushin , Manuel Arto . All at Nethermind. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . TL;DR EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100k; too low for a Groth16 privacy transfer or post-quantum signatures . Raising the cap is a DoS risk, since validation and block processing share the node’s CPU. An attacker can send transactions that use the whole cap and then fail, taking CPU from block processing for free. We tested this risk on a Nethermind node, flooding it with such transactions at caps from 100k to 500k, on one CPU core (the worst case) and three machines. Without in-client protections, block processing on our slowest machine stays within a 25 ms delay budget only up to 15M gas/s. With Nethermind allowing up to about 100 failing tx/s per connection, that limits the cap to the current 100k. We show that a MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 300k is viable with an in-client protection that pauses transaction validation while the node processes a block. At 100 tx/s (30M gas/s), block processing then stays within 50 ms, even on p90 mainnet blocks. The cost moves to the mempool, which admits only 12–27% of honest frame transactions under the flood. 1. Introduction In an ordinary Ethereum transaction the signature check is cheap and fixed. In an EIP-8141 frame transaction the check is arbitrary EVM code in a VERIFY frame.
