events.excerpt: Daniil Ankushin, Nethermind. Verify-budget figures: method by Daniil Ankushin, benchmark and measurements by Manuel Arto. On frame transactions a shielded pool pays its own gas, so a private withdrawal needs no relayer. We ran a real BN254 Groth16 pool this way on current Nethermind master: a withdrawal costs 679,322 gas. With EIP-8250 nonce keys, many withdrawals can come from the one pool address at once. Two things do not work yet. The proof check is over the spec cap on validation gas, and a pool cannot pay for a call from the user’s own address. The pool we ran is soispoke’s minimal-shielded-pool ( GitHub - soispoke/minimal-shielded-pool · GitHub ). How a withdrawal works In a withdrawal the pool is the sender. Its VERIFY code checks the zk proof and approves execution and payment. The user needs no funded account and does not appear in the transaction. Two drafts make this safe in a public mempool. With EIP-8250 the pool uses the note’s nullifiers as nonce keys. Each withdrawal has its own nonce key, so withdrawals with the pool as sender do not compete for one nonce. A side effect: a nullifier that was already used is a used nonce key, so the protocol refuses a double spend before the pool’s code runs. With EIP-8272 the transaction checks the pool’s Merkle root against a contract of recent roots before the pool’s code runs, so a mempool node never reads the pool’s storage. It sat in public source the whole time. I audit smart contracts, not browser extensions, but the review lessons carry over to any code that touches keys. The function that matters is about 25 lines, in a new 180 line file, inside a diff of almost 11,000 changed lines whose title says it adds TON. It left the same way. The code was deleted from the source on 25 June 2026, inside a release commit with about 80,000 changed lines. What each piece looked like in a diff The name. On every unlock the extension calls fetchJettonInfo() . Jettons are TON tokens, so in a TON PR that reads like a token info fetch. events.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture. The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That
events.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture

events.excerpt: Hi all. We recently opened a discussion in the Solana SIMD repository about a new class of smart contracts we’re loosely calling “inference programs,” or “Actually Smart Contracts.” We’d value technical input from this community on whether a similar proposal could be feasible on Ethereum, before we write anything for it. The idea, briefly: a contract stores a prompt and the rules that shape it (a DAO constitution, a policy, a standard). Another contract asks it a question with evidence. AI models from different operators answer off chain, each signs a vote, and the caller checks the signed result before acting. The motivator was Anthropic’s recent work on zero-knowledge proofs of LLM inference . The Solana drafts and the discussion so far: Overview and drafts: Bringing Inference Programs To Solana Microsite with diagrams and a sandbox: asc.verafy.ai Discussion: solana-improvement-documents #724 We have no strong view on whether this is technically feasible, and we know there is a lot of prior work here that we may not have accounted for, including optimistic oracles and opML. The drafts were written with help from AI tools, so some of it may be poorly reasoned. The questions we’d most like help with: Is this better as an application-level ERC, or not a standard at all? Proofs of inference are currently far too large to verify on chain (about 18.78 MB each). Is a commit, bond and challenge design the realistic path on Ethereum, or is there a better one? What existing work should we build on or defer to instead? Thank you for any pointers. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full t
events.title: Would an ERC for inference programs (AI-evaluated contracts) be feasible on Ethereum?

events.excerpt: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work. Accessibility statements make project practices visible GitHub CLI’s accessibility statemen
events.title: Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub

events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. Instead of deploying a new contract for each program, callers provide the program as calldata. The proxy temporarily caches the program and forwards it to an implementation that interprets and executes it. This design provides several benefits: Dynamic execution programs: Different programs can be supplied for different execution sessions without deploying a new contract. events.title: ERC-8486: Flash Loan Proxy

events.excerpt: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President ( AS2650 ). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period. The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica , a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications . Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge. events.excerpt: Proposal Type: Protocol Upgrade Hi, I’m Andrea Federici, Senior Solutions Engineer at OP Labs. I prepared this proposal in collaboration with Matthew Cruz from the OP Labs team. Neither OP Labs nor I, nor any other entity mentioned, represent or speak on behalf of the Optimism Foundation. Executive Summary Upgrade 21 is an L1 smart contract upgrade for OP Stack chains, shipped in op-contracts/v9.0.0 . It has no hardfork and no activation timestamp: every change is applied through a signed superchain-ops execution on L1. It contains the following changes: ETHLockbox as custody and pause identifier — every chain gets an ETHLockbox that cannot be disabled, and it becomes the only identifier for a chain-specific pause. Chains whose ETH is still in the OptimismPortal have it moved into the lockbox in the upgrade transaction. Chains that already use a lockbox are unchanged. Custom gas token chains get a lockbox but keep custody in the portal. Permissionless deleteProvenWithdrawal — anyone can delete a withdrawal proof whose dispute game resolved in favor of the challenger or was blacklisted. Proofs on valid games are unaffected. OPCM v9.0.0 and StandardValidator — removes the startingAnchorRoot upgrade override, lowers batched-upgrade gas, and adds validator checks for the new lockbox and pause configuration. events.excerpt: Release Notes Node version 11.2.0 is a pre-release version of cardano-node that is not yet recommended for use on mainnet. Its headline change is the move to the new cardano-config library for reading node configuration: the node now understands a versioned configuration "envelope" alongside the existing flat format, and the configuration files published for each network are now in the envelope format. It also extends the gRPC interface, continues the groundwork for the Dijkstra era, Leios and Peras, and fixes several operator-facing bugs. Highlights: New configuration format. Configurations are read through cardano-config . Existing flat configurations still work. The new envelope format ( $schema / Version / MinNodeVersion / Configuration ) is schema-validated. New cardano-node config migrate , cardano-node config schema and cardano-node config resolve subcommands convert, describe and check a configuration. The shipped network configs are now enveloped and cannot be read by nodes older than 11.2 . gRPC over HTTP/2. The gRPC server can now listen on a TCP address/port, in plaintext (h2c) or with TLS ( --grpc-listen-address / --grpc-listen-port , --grpc-tls-* ), instead of only a unix socket. New gRPC methods ReadMempool , WatchMempool and ReadEraSummary , plus server reflection. Node-to-client versions older than NodeToClientV_23 are no longer supported. Clients (wallets, indexers, tools) must be built against a version of the network libraries that speaks NodeToClientV_23 (shipped since node 10.7.0). Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. By reformulating broadcast access control as a homomorphic blind Reed–Solomon decoding problem over 𝔽 256 using carry-free Base-3 packing in exponential ElGamal ciphertexts (𝔾 1 × 𝔾 1 ), Stealth ABBE achieves: O(1) Broadcast KEM Size (24.1 KiB amortized): Fits comfortably inside a single EIP-4844 blob (~19% of one 128 KiB blob) regardless of the total participant count N . Zero Visible Headers or Revocation Lists (0 Bytes): Access policies, cohort rosters, and revocation states are algebraically absorbed into the non-systematic Reed–Solomon codeword. Uniform Noise Indistinguishability (STAC Paradigm): Using explicit inverse isogenies and Elligator Squared over 𝔾 1 , the entire broadcast frame is statistically indistinguishable from uniform channel noise, defeating mempool/blob Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) and cohort g
events.title: Stealth ABBE over BLS12-381: Zero-Metadata Broadcast of Private Contracts & Encrypted State via EIP-4844 Blobs
